title: Al-Ghashiyah: look at the camel
hook: don't they look at the camel, the sky, the mountains, the earth spread out (88:17–20)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Ghashiyah, the overwhelming, and the two kinds of faces. Your line was which face.

Day two hundred. That's a lot of mornings. So here's a question for this one: what did you see on your way here today? Not what was there. What did you see? It's easy to move through a day like a video playing with the sound off: trees, sky, a dog, a building, all of it wallpaper. Halfway through, Al-Ghashiyah does something unexpected. It stops talking about the next world and points at four very ordinary things in this one, starting with an animal its first listeners saw every day. Today: look at the camel.
screen: `WHAT DID YOU SEE TODAY?` → `THE WORLD AS WALLPAPER.` → `LOOK AT THE CAMEL.`

segments.voice: Verse seventeen, in Pickthall's words: Will they not regard the camels, how they are created? Then: and the sky, how it is raised. And the mountains, how they are set up. And the earth, how it is spread out. Picture the first listeners, in Mecca. Camels were part of daily life: transport, milk, wealth, the animal tied up outside the house. And the surah says: look at it. How was it made? An animal that crosses a desert carrying loads, going days without water. Then lift your eyes to the sky. Then the horizon, the mountains, fixed. Then down at your feet, ground spread flat enough to walk on and build on. Near, above, far, below: a full turn of the head. The argument is quiet. It doesn't list proofs. It asks you to pay attention, trusting that attention itself leads somewhere. Then verse twenty-one, a line for the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and for anyone who wants to share what they believe: so remind, for you are only a reminder. Verse twenty-two: you are not a controller over them. The word is musaytir, someone with authority to force. The Prophet's job, the surah says, was to point, like pointing at a camel: look. Not to make anyone see. Some readers take a rule of thumb from that line: the one who reminds is responsible for the reminding, not for what the other person does with it.
screen: `CAMEL, SKY, MOUNTAINS, EARTH.` · `AN EVERYDAY ANIMAL IN MECCA.` · `NEAR, ABOVE, FAR, BELOW.` · `A REMINDER, NOT A CONTROLLER.` · then, large: `LOOK AT THE CAMEL.`

segments.voice: Do the full turn of the head: first one thing near you, an object, a plant, your own hand, looked at as if you'd never seen one. Then the sky, or the ceiling if that's what's above you, then the farthest thing you can see, then the ground under you. Four things, looked at properly.
Al-Ghashiyah. The overwhelming, Surah eighty-eight, which pauses to say: look at the camel, the sky, the mountains, the earth. Today's word.
Your line: look at the camel. Attention comes first. Two hundred days, and still looking.

howItsDone: Muslims speak of tafakkur, reflective looking at creation, as a form of worship; the camel verses of Al-Ghashiyah are often quoted to invite it.

myth: the camel was an exotic animal to the first listeners
it was an everyday animal in Mecca, which is the point.

remind, for you are only a reminder; you are not a controller over them (88:21–22).

fork.setup: after the camel, sky, mountains and earth, the surah turns to the Prophet. what is his job?
fork.reveal: remind, for you are only a reminder; you are not a controller over them. to point at the camel, not to force anyone to see.

original.note: Arabic: camels, a collective noun with no singular form of its own; one camel is jamal or naqah.

trapdoor: what you thought: camels are interesting animals.
what it means: look closely at the near, the high, the far and the ground under you; attention is the first step.
what a scholar hears: afala yanzuruna, will they not look; then mudhakkir against musaytir in 88:21–22, a verse often cited on the limits of compulsion in calling others to faith.

ibil as a collective with no singular of its own (jamal, naqah used for one): confirm.
